column1: Built-in REGEXP_* functions were introduced in SQL Server {{c1::2025}}.
column2:
SQL Server 2022 does not have these built-ins. Check the database compatibility requirement for the particular function.
Review source

column1: The regex quantifier {{c1::*}} means zero or more repetitions of the preceding expression.
column2:
The match can include no b at all, one b, or a run of b characters. The operator applies only to the preceding expression.
Review source

column1: The regex quantifier {{c1::+}} means one or more repetitions of the preceding expression.
column2:
The match starts with at least one b in that position. The example therefore matches abc but not ac.
Review source

column1: The regex quantifier {{c1::?}} makes the preceding expression optional.
column2:
For example, colou?r matches color and colour. It does not allow two copies of the optional u.
Review source

column1: With the m flag absent, the regex anchor {{c1::^}} requires the beginning of the input text.
column2:
Without multiline mode, this requires a match at the start of the entire input rather than at an internal line start.
Review source

column1: With the m flag absent, the regex anchor {{c1::$}} requires the end of the input text.
column2:
Without multiline mode, the end position belongs to the full input rather than every line.
Review source

column1: The regex character class {{c1::[abc]}} matches one a, b, or c.
column2:
The brackets offer alternatives for one position. They do not require the sequence abc.
Review source

column1: The regex character class {{c1::[^0-9]}} matches one character that is not an ASCII digit.
column2:
The caret negates the class only in this position inside the brackets. A letter can match, but 7 cannot.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server regex, {{c1::\d}} is shorthand for [0-9].
column2:
The class covers ASCII digits. Add a quantifier such as + if you want to collect an entire digit run.
Review source

column1: Exactly four repetitions of the preceding regex expression use the quantifier {{c1::{4}}}.
column2:
For example, use it after a digit class to require exactly four digits. Put parentheses around a longer unit if the whole unit must repeat.
Review source

column1: Between two and four repetitions of the preceding regex expression use the quantifier {{c1::{2,4}}}.
column2:
Two, three, or four occurrences satisfy the range. One and five fall outside it when the pattern must match the full input.
Review source

column1: The regex operator {{c1::|}} provides alternation, as in cat|dog.
column2:
For example, use anchors around a grouped alternative to validate either full word, not just a substring.
Review source

column1: To match a literal period rather than a wildcard, use the regex pattern {{c1::\.}}.
column2:
The escape takes away the dot's wildcard meaning. It matches the punctuation mark itself.
Review source

column1: Capture a digit run with the regex group {{c1::(\d+)}}.
column2:
The parentheses capture the run as one group. The plus requires one or more digits in that run.
Review source

column1: SQL Server regex uses flag {{c1::c}} for its default case-sensitive matching.
column2:
The default distinguishes lower- and uppercase letters. Specify i when a pattern needs case-insensitive matching.
Review source

column1: Case-insensitive SQL Server regex matching uses flag {{c1::i}}.
column2:
With i, frame and Frame can both match. This choice comes from the regex flags, not SQL collation rules.
Review source

column1: SQL Server regex flag {{c1::s}} allows . to match a newline.
column2:
The flag changes the dot wildcard's behavior. Use m separately when anchors need to recognize line boundaries.
Review source

column1: SQL Server regex flag {{c1::m}} lets ^ and $ match line boundaries within multiline text.
column2:
This changes where the anchors can match. It does not make the dot wildcard include a newline.
Review source

column1: Swap Smith, John to John Smith with REGEXP_REPLACE('Smith, John','^(\w+),\s*(\w+)$',{{c1::'\2 \1'}}).
column2:
The replacement inserts group 2 first and group 1 second. Group references in replacement text are not matching-pattern backreferences.
Review source

column1: Collapse whitespace runs to one space with REGEXP_REPLACE(@s,{{c1::'\s+'}},' ').
column2:
The pattern consumes one run of whitespace at a time. The replacement puts a single space where each run was found.
Review source

column1: Extract the second digit run with REGEXP_SUBSTR(@s,'\d+',1,{{c1::2}}).
column2:
The function skips the first matching run and returns the second. If there is no second run, it returns NULL.
Review source

column1: Extract an email domain without @ using REGEXP_SUBSTR(@email,'@(.+)$',1,1,'c',{{c1::1}}).
column2:
The whole match starts with @. Selecting group 1 discards that prefix because it is outside the parentheses.
Review source

column1: REGEXP_INSTR('AB12','\d') returns {{c1::3}}.
column2:
Count positions starting at one. The two letters occupy positions one and two, so the first digit starts at three.
Review source

column1: Count digit runs in @s with {{c1::REGEXP_COUNT(@s,'\d+')}}.
column2:
A sequence like 345 contributes one match, not three. To count individual digits, use a pattern without the run quantifier.
Review source

column1: Split on commas, semicolons, or pipes with REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE(@s,{{c1::'[,;|]'}}).
column2:
Each delimiter is one allowed character inside the brackets. The pipe there is not an alternation operator.
Review source

column1: Return split tokens in input order with SELECT value FROM REGEXP_SPLIT_TO_TABLE(@s,',') {{c1::ORDER BY ordinal}}.
column2:
The order clause sorts the returned token rows by their recorded positions. The function's rowset alone does not guarantee display order.
Review source
